isp-counterparty: ESP makes the ISP the household's financial counterparty for participating Internet services
apps earn through the protocol instead of establishing a separate billing relationship with every household
app-set-prices: ESP explicitly chooses app-set prices over Spotify-style fixed-pot sharing
each app sets its tariff, and evidenced consumption at accepted prices determines its claim
revenue is not a share of a fixed subscription pool
internet-bill: the household pays its ISP under one standing plan
only the agreed plan price and any separately priced add-on explicitly accepted by the household may be charged
standing-plan: The household buys predictable access rather than a sequence of isolated purchases
allowing light and heavy usage to vary without turning every online act into a separate household bill
monthly-epochs: The architecture runs in monthly epochs
disputes resolve inside a defined window, and settlement executes once
funding-pressure: App prices transmit rising service costs into ISP funding pressure
Price pressure does not bypass retail or funding limits
putting pressure on the ISP to raise future household plan prices
price-feedback: ESP chooses user experience as the household's immediate economic feedback
Economic feedback from app prices works through household user experience
Household analytics make the cost of app choices visible
fup-faucet: Fair-use policy is implemented as an allowance faucet
the request carries no amount and the ISP alone decides how much to grant
the protocol defines no remaining-grant-capacity field, grant-sizing formula or tail-reserve rule
base-and-topups: Every activated household has one fungible monthly allowance
The base allowance is guaranteed while top-ups are conditional
retail-contract: The ISP's subscriber contract defines the retail promise
The protocol deliberately leaves retail product design outside consensus
signed-refusal: the signed refusal gives the household evidence if the ISP instead breaks the retail promise it sold
a refusal during a hot month is legitimate when it follows the subscribed FUP
common-fund: ESP operates one common protocol-level fund
The total pots assigned across all ISPs cannot exceed the common fund's liquid backing
The common fund can lose money only through actual ISP default
isp-commitment: Each ISP prepays one aggregate monthly commitment
they are ISP-declared funding attributions, not household allowances
the-pot: The protocol assigns each ISP a monthly pot
the pot is spending authority, not money transferred to the ISP
The pot is the ISP's non-negotiable solvency boundary
overdraft: The pot may be larger than the ISP's commitments
the difference is the ISP overdraft allocation
New ISPs receive no unsecured overdraft by default
isp-debt: Debt arises only from executed consumption
Debt preserves financial accountability while allowing temporary support
Persistent heavy consumption must return to the ISP's own economics
debt-update: The ISP's debt is updated mechanically
New communal surplus is recognized only after the ISP's opening debt has been repaid
Every capital-account update is publicly reproducible
Debt-service payments create no new allowance or pot capacity
price-catalogue: Each app publishes one signed price catalogue for the epoch
Accepted prices remain fixed for the epoch
The epoch price-catalogue mechanism in section 4 awaits incorporation
conrec: Every billable act produces a Consumption Record (ConRec) signed by both economic parties
the household signs with its epoch key, the app countersigns and attests the time
optimistic-serving: an app may accept the risk of serving against a household-signed ConRec that exceeds the allowance then in force
evidence-kept: Price agreements and fine-grained evidence remain off-chain during ordinary operation
apps retain accepted tariff agreements and ConRecs needed to prove their claims
the box retains its complete ConRec diary and each app retains the ConRecs it served
hsatm: Every allowance decision becomes a jointly signed historical fact
carrying the epoch, sequence number, timestamp, and new total, signed by both the ISP and the household's box
the highest-sequence HSATM carries the authoritative Household Signed Allowance Total (HSAT)
box-hlaa: The normal box enforces the allowance locally
it declines to sign consumption beyond the authorized total
the box's household-local allowance account combines that total with signed consumption
heid: The box creates the epoch identity before the ISP declares the household
the box generates a new keypair, the public key becomes the household epoch ID (HEID)
epoch-opening: Epoch opening follows one required dependency order
A rostered household defaults to zero allowance until it is activated
Incomplete household activation does not rewrite the funded epoch
hpc: The Household Participation Credential (HPC) is the required app-facing admission proof
an app verifies the ISP signature, matches the epoch and HEID, and verifies that the household controls the corresponding private key
The credential discloses neither the household's allowance nor its HCD contribution attribution
identity-layers: The identity model has three deliberate layers
Only the parent ISP can resolve a public claim to a household
the parent ISP normally sees only per-app household aggregates needed for reconciliation
encrypted-heids: Fresh encryption randomness prevents public basket reconstruction
two apps claiming against the same household produce unlinkable ciphertexts
each public claim row contains the household's HEID encrypted with the parent ISP's public key
verification-tag: The ISP and box also share one private verification secret
The AtS verification tag gives a household visibility without giving apps a lookup table
A tag-to-ciphertext substitution is detected and evidenced after the fact
the box detects a shaved amount through its verification tag and latest HSATM
ats: The public Allowance to Spend (AtS) is anonymous but self-verifiable
Each ISP posts one closing allowance list for the epoch
The AtS is a closing report rather than a live spending oracle
ishec: The household independently checks both sides of its monthly equation
The IsHEC must reach the household while payment can still be stopped
epoch-timetable: The epoch timetable prevents races and premature sweeps
App claims have a hard deadline
Blockchain load scales with participants and disputes rather than usage volume
The fixed epoch footprint is explicit
hcd: The HCD is the protocol-facing funding step inside epoch opening
the ISP-signed HCD is authoritative for roster membership and the protocol trusts the ISP's declaration
Roster authenticity is an explicit ISP trust boundary
rtgp: Each app converts many service requests into one monthly claim
Every app's Request to get Paid (RtgP) carries publicly checkable ISP subtotals
reconcile-together: The ISP reconciles all accepted app claims together rather than processing them in arrival order
cannot favor an early app by spending the allowance before later claims arrive
heea: A household escrow account is an accounting container, not a separate money transfer
the household epoch escrow account (HEEA) caps what may be paid for one household in one epoch
iptd: The IPtD publishes settlement outcomes without exposing household app baskets
Public verification checks arithmetic without repeating the ISP's private reconciliation
the ISP publishes each app's proposed payout, its flagged rows, the aggregate amount charged, and the remainder
freeze-settle: Clean households settle and flagged households freeze
an aggregate above the cap stops every row for that household and automatically opens an evidence round before any of those rows are paid
Freezing an overrun normally prevents fraudulent money from leaving the fund
isp-epoch-failure: Failure to open or close an ISP epoch has explicit consequences
a missed AtS, unpaid required debt service, or unfunded allowance correction establishes an ISP default
Collateral slashing and forced wind-down remain intended consequences, but the machinery that imposes them is deferred
who-does-what: The household box is an observer in ordinary operation
The ISP is trusted with private mapping and computation but not with payment discretion
Apps are both service providers and evidence custodians
evidence-round: An evidence round can arise from three provable triggers
A Call for Evidence turns the dispute into a bounded public proceeding
Evidence responses deliberately reveal one disputed household's epoch basket
mechanical-resolution: Resolution is designed to be mechanical rather than discretionary
The ISP supplies the authoritative witness list
False inclusion in an evidence call is self-correcting
escalation-audit: An unsupported row is voided, but missing evidence alone does not prove fabrication
that is app fraud and escalates into an audit of the app's entire epoch
An escalation audit follows the app across every retained claim it can still be required to prove
silent-padding: Silent padding hides a fabricated app charge below the household's HEEA
Ordinary silent padding is exposed through overlapping signals
Allowance lookup would enable targeted silent padding
household-fraud: Valid consumption beyond the closing allowance is household fraud
the household escrow is divided among the valid app claims in proportion to their amounts
A dishonest household cannot make the common fund exceed its funded exposure
allowance-correction: A false closing entry cannot be used to convict an honest household
An allowance correction first uses pot capacity already reserved for the ISP
timing-states: The ex-post audit separates two timing states
End-state FUP audits are arbitrated by the ESP protocol
Spend-ahead consumes future allowance before the ISP grants it
Those timestamps do not independently prove the actual signing order
hoarding: Allowance hoarding can distort the ISP's internal grant allocation
Hoarding and spend-ahead are contractual violations even if later events make the final arithmetic fit
epoch-opening-handoff: the exact bilateral transport for the control proof remains unspecified
ats-binding-challenge: The AtS-binding challenge route and remedy remain unsealed
the submission route, adjudicating actor, challenge deadline, privacy boundary, correction or recovery remedy, and penalty consequence remain deferred
pre-activation-conrec: Pre-activation ConRec enforcement and auditability remain unsealed
The current evidence does not prove that admission preceded a ConRec
tariff-format: Epoch tariff agreements still need a format and evidence specification
credit-calibration: The ISP credit policy still needs numerical calibration
Unresolved debt-control rules may eventually raise an ISP's aggregate HCD requirement
The exact formula, thresholds and number of epochs remain TODO
collusion-padding: ISP-and-app collusion still has an undefeated silent-padding form
anti-collusion: Several future anti-collusion mechanisms remain candidates
borrow-and-default: Borrow-and-default replaces consumption-weighted allocation farming as the central common-fund attack
durable-second-instance: The end state needs a durable second instance
the design still must define how household evidence reaches the protocol, how a dispute involving an ISP is decided
finality-horizon: Finality and post-execution recovery remain unsealed
Settlement finality after execution is deferred
The exact retention period is deferred with settlement finality and recovery
penalty-enforcement: Collateral slashing and forced wind-down remain intended consequences, but the machinery that imposes them is deferred
proven app and ISP violations are intended to lead to slashing or expulsion under the deferred penalty-enforcement design
App registration collateral remains part of the intended end state
isp-fronting: The pro-rata household-shortfall rule may be reconsidered only in a future revision
emergency-settlement: A missing IPtD requires an emergency-settlement route
How a second instance reconstructs the required claim assignments, executes emergency settlement, and imposes those consequences remains undefined
how settlement is recovered when the ISP fails a required duty
household-routes: Household ingress, independent dispute resolution and emergency recovery remain separate end-state TODOs
The eventual household-to-protocol challenge route remains unsealed
The production-demand and escalation routes remain unresolved
future household transparency, whose mechanism remains undefined
Exceptional evidence submission remains an unresolved route
audit-design: The proof relation, committed policy inputs, proof-generation and protocol-verification interface, completeness guarantee and any fallback disclosure are not yet designed
The invocation route, standing, deadlines, result record and connection to ISP-household contractual remedies remain deferred
the audit mechanism, proof duties, disclosure boundary and authoritative result remain deferred
detection-posture: The fraud posture is detection plus consequences rather than universal real-time prevention
signed evidence makes later reconstruction possible, caps bound interim exposure
